explanations.answer: After they enter the land He's giving them
explanations.explanation: That's the timing, friend. The LORD says, "After you enter the land that I am giving you as a home…" (Numbers 15:2). Notice He's already talking about a home they haven't reached yet. I know a little about waiting for a new place, so I like hearing it.

explanations.answer: While they wander in the wilderness
explanations.explanation: Close, because the wilderness is where they are right now. But the LORD says these instructions start "After you enter the land that I am giving you as a home…" (Numbers 15:2). So the wandering isn't the starting line. The land is.

explanations.answer: Once the forty years are halfway done
explanations.explanation: I get why you'd reach for a number, friend. But the text gives no halfway mark here. The LORD says it starts "After you enter the land that I am giving you as a home…" (Numbers 15:2). The moment is the land, not a point on the calendar.
Yes, friend. The text says the foreigner "is to do exactly as you do" (Numbers 15:14). No side door, no special version. If you're bringing it, you're bringing it the same way.

explanations.answer: With half the flour and oil
explanations.explanation: Nice try, but nobody gets a smaller scoop. The text says the foreigner "is to do exactly as you do" (Numbers 15:14). Same flour, same oil, same everything. A shortcut recipe is how you get a sad cookie, and the LORD isn't handing out shortcuts here.
That would be a limit, and the text doesn't set one. It says the foreigner "is to do exactly as you do" (Numbers 15:14). Whatever the Israelites do, he does. No extra fine print.
That's the word. The LORD says, "it is a permanent statute for the generations to come" (Numbers 15:15). He adds, "You and the foreigner shall be the same before the LORD." One law, and it stays.

I can see why that might sound right, since they're still wandering. But the text says the opposite: "it is a permanent statute for the generations to come" (Numbers 15:15). It's not a sticky note on the fridge. It's carved in.
Friend, this one isn't a take-it-or-leave-it buffet. The text calls it "a permanent statute for the generations to come" (Numbers 15:15). And it's the same one for the native-born and the foreigner.

Yes, dough! The LORD says, "From the first of your dough, you are to lift up a cake as a contribution" (Numbers 15:20). Of everything on that list, this is the one that gets my mustache twitching. The first batch goes to Him.

Wine does show up in this passage, friend, but as a drink offering alongside the animals (Numbers 15:5). The "first of" offering is something else. The LORD says, "From the first of your dough, you are to lift up a cake as a contribution" (Numbers 15:20).

explanations.answer: The first of their olive oil
explanations.explanation: Olive oil is in the passage too, mixed into the flour for the grain offerings (Numbers 15:4). But the "first of" offering isn't the oil. The LORD says, "From the first of your dough, you are to lift up a cake as a contribution" (Numbers 15:20).

I see the logic, friend, since it does begin with their first dough. But read on. The LORD says, "Throughout your generations, you are to give the LORD an offering from the first of your dough" (Numbers 15:21). So it isn't a one-time gift. It keeps going, generation after generation.

That's right, friend. The LORD says, "Throughout your generations, you are to give the LORD an offering from the first of your dough" (Numbers 15:21). It's not a one-and-done. Every generation gives from the first of its dough.

explanations.answer: One young bull and one male goat
explanations.explanation: That's it. The whole congregation is to prepare "one young bull as a burnt offering" with its grain offering and drink offering, "and one male goat as a sin offering" (Numbers 15:24). One bull, one goat. Easy to count, hard to forget.

Sevens do show up in the Bible, friend, but not here. For the whole congregation's unintentional sin, it's "one young bull as a burnt offering" and "one male goat as a sin offering" (Numbers 15:24). One and one, no big pile.

explanations.answer: Two lambs and a pair of doves
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a nice combo, but it's not this one. The text says "one young bull as a burnt offering" and "one male goat as a sin offering" (Numbers 15:24). No lambs, no doves in this verse.
Yes, friend. The text says the priest makes atonement "so that they may be forgiven; for the sin was unintentional" (Numbers 15:25). That's good news, and I'll take it every time.
Scattered sounds like a bag of sprinkles hitting the floor, friend, but that's not what happens here. The priest makes atonement "so that they may be forgiven" (Numbers 15:25). Forgiven is the word.
I get the guess, since this passage is full of rules. But the text says the priest makes atonement "so that they may be forgiven" (Numbers 15:25). Nothing here about a test. They're forgiven.

True, friend. The text says, "Then the whole congregation of Israel and the foreigners residing among them will be forgiven, since it happened to all the people unintentionally" (Numbers 15:26). The foreigners are named right in the verse. Nobody is left standing at the door.

Not false, friend. The text says, "Then the whole congregation of Israel and the foreigners residing among them will be forgiven, since it happened to all the people unintentionally" (Numbers 15:26). The foreigners are in that sentence, forgiven right along with everyone else.

That's the one. "If one person sins unintentionally, he is to present a year-old female goat as a sin offering" (Numbers 15:27). Notice it's a different animal than the congregation's bull and goat. One person, one goat.
A year-old animal, yes, but the wrong one. The text says "a year-old female goat as a sin offering" (Numbers 15:27). A lamb is a fine animal, but this verse doesn't ask for one.

explanations.answer: A young bull from the herd
explanations.explanation: The young bull is for the whole congregation (Numbers 15:24), so it's a good mix-up, friend. For one person the text says "a year-old female goat as a sin offering" (Numbers 15:27). Smaller group, different animal.

I see why you'd wonder, since the passage keeps naming both groups. But the LORD says, "You shall have the same law for the one who acts in error, whether he is a native-born Israelite or a foreigner residing among you" (Numbers 15:29). So it's the same law, not a different one.

Right, friend. The LORD says, "You shall have the same law for the one who acts in error, whether he is a native-born Israelite or a foreigner residing among you" (Numbers 15:29). One law covers both. No second rulebook.

That's what the text says. "But the person who sins defiantly, whether a native or foreigner, blasphemes the LORD" (Numbers 15:30). This is a heavy part, friend. The text treats defiance very differently from an accident.

Hiding is a human thing to do, friend. I think a lot of us have wanted to duck out of sight. But this verse doesn't say it. It says the person who sins defiantly "blasphemes the LORD" (Numbers 15:30).
Forgetting sounds close, but it's the opposite side of the line. Straying unintentionally is what the earlier verses cover (Numbers 15:22). The defiant person "blasphemes the LORD" (Numbers 15:30).

That would erase the line the LORD just drew, friend. For the one who strays unintentionally, the priest makes atonement and he "will be forgiven" (Numbers 15:28). But of the defiant person, the text says, "That person shall be cut off from among his people" (Numbers 15:30). It's not the same.

Yes, and it's a heavy one, friend. The text says the defiant person "shall be cut off from among his people" (Numbers 15:30). It ends with "his guilt remains on him" (Numbers 15:31). That's very different from the one who strayed unintentionally.

explanations.answer: He despised the word of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives. "He shall certainly be cut off, because he has despised the word of the LORD and broken His commandment" (Numbers 15:31). It's a serious verse, friend, and I won't joke on it.

explanations.answer: He defiled the camp of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Defiling the camp is a phrase from other places, friend, but it's not what this verse says. The reason given is, "because he has despised the word of the LORD and broken His commandment" (Numbers 15:31). This is a heavy one, so I'm sticking close to the text.

explanations.answer: He neglected the feasts of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Feasts do come up earlier, in the offerings (Numbers 15:3). But that's not the reason here. The text says, "because he has despised the word of the LORD and broken His commandment" (Numbers 15:31). It's a heavy verse, so I'll keep it simple.
